:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The round three-sphere is the most symmetric left-invariant metric, and it must reproduce the curvature computed in
Part I in Euler angles. The first example makes this comparison.

::: {#exm-vcr-lic-round}
#### The round sphere

For $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = \tfrac12$ the metric is $\tfrac14\sum_a\sigma_a^2$, the metric @eq-su2-metric of the unit
three-sphere, and @eq-vcr-bianchi-ix-curvature gives $R = \tfrac{3}{16}\big/\tfrac{1}{32} = 6$, the value of @prp-su2-curvature.
The frame Ricci components are all $\operatorname{Ric}(e_a, e_a) = \tfrac12 = 2a_a^2$, so $\operatorname{Ric} = 2g$: an
Einstein metric.
:::

Squashing the sphere along the Hopf fibre keeps a $U(2)$ symmetry and gives the Berger spheres. The example shows that
their curvature becomes negative for strong squashing, which is impossible for a round sphere.

::: {#exm-vcr-lic-berger}
#### Berger spheres

With $a_1 = a_2 = a$, $a_3 = b$, @eq-vcr-bianchi-ix-curvature becomes $R = (4a^2 - b^2)/(2a^4)$, positive for $b <
2a$, zero for $b = 2a$ and negative beyond (@exr-vcr-lic-berger-sage). The fibre direction $e_3$ has
$\operatorname{Ric}(e_3, e_3) = b^4/(2a^4) > 0$ at all squashings, while the base directions have $(2a^2 - b^2)/(2a^2)$,
negative for $b > \sqrt2a$: a stretched Hopf fibre gives the sign pattern of the nilmanifold
(@exr-vcr-lic-heis-curvature).
:::

In the reduced theory the scalars $a_a$ are fields, and the curvature is their potential. The example identifies the
round sphere as the stationary point of that potential at fixed volume, which @fig-vcr-group-manifold displays.

::: {#exm-vcr-lic-potential}
#### The scalar potential

Reducing $-\hat R$ on @eq-vcr-gm-ansatz gives a potential proportional to $-R(g_{ab})$ times powers of the volume,
quadratic in the structure constants [@hull2005, eq. 4.7]. At fixed volume, $-R = \tfrac12t^4 - 2t$ has its minimum at
the round sphere, $t = 1$, with $-R = -\tfrac32$: a negative contribution to the vacuum energy and a stable shape modulus, while the volume
modulus still needs another contribution to be fixed. Because $R$ is constant on $SU(2)$, no
equation of motion depends on the point of the group.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The constancy of the frame components is a general fact, not a property of $SU(2)$. The first exercise proves it with
Cartan's structure equations of @sec-connections-curvature.

::: {#exr-vcr-lic-frame}
#### Why the curvature is constant

For an orthonormal frame $e^a = L^a{}_b\sigma^b$ with constant $L$, show that $de^a = -\tfrac12C_{bc}{}^ae^b \wedge e^c$
with constant $C$, that the connection one-forms $\omega^a{}_b$ solving $de^a + \omega^a{}_b \wedge e^b = 0$ have
constant frame components, and conclude that every frame component of the curvature is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$de^a = L^a{}_bd\sigma^b = -\tfrac12L^a{}_bf_{cd}{}^b\sigma^c \wedge \sigma^d$, and substituting $\sigma = L^{-1}e$
gives constant $C$. The torsion-free metric connection is unique, and the Koszul formula gives its frame components $\omega_{abc}$ as a
fixed linear combination of the $C_{abc}$ (indices lowered with $\delta$), so they are constants;
$\Omega^a{}_b = d\omega^a{}_b + \omega^a{}_c \wedge \omega^c{}_b$ then contains $d\omega = \omega_{\cdot\cdot c}de^c$,
again constant in the frame. Hence $\operatorname{Ric}(e_a, e_b)$ and $R$ are constants, quadratic in $C$.
:::

The Berger family can be computed directly in Sage with the Euler-angle forms. The second exercise asks for the
scalar curvature and the frame Ricci matrix.

::: {#exr-vcr-lic-berger-sage}
#### The Berger sphere in Sage

With SageManifolds, compute the scalar curvature and the frame Ricci matrix of $a^2(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2) +
b^2\sigma_3^2$, and find the squashing at which $R$ changes sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R = (4a^2 - b^2)/(2a^4)$ changes sign at $b = 2a$; the frame Ricci matrix is $\operatorname{diag}((2a^2 -
b^2)/(2a^2), (2a^2 - b^2)/(2a^2), b^4/(2a^4))$, with all entries free of the angles:

{{< sage exr-vcr-lic-berger-sage >}}
:::

The nilmanifold is the opposite case: its curvature is negative for every twist. The last exercise computes it and
reads off what the potential does to the twist.

::: {#exr-vcr-lic-heis-curvature}
#### The nilmanifold

With SageManifolds, compute the scalar curvature of $dy^2 + (dz^2)^2 + (dz^1 + my\,dz^2)^2$ and its frame Ricci matrix.
What is the sign of the potential $-R$, and does it have a stationary point in $m$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R = -\tfrac12m^2$ with frame Ricci matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-\tfrac12, \tfrac12, -\tfrac12)m^2$, independent of
$y$ as the proposition predicts. The potential $-R = \tfrac12m^2$ is positive and, once the moduli $g_{ab}$ are restored, it scales like an inverse
power of the sizes of the base: it has no stationary point at non-zero twist and pushes the moduli towards a large
base:

{{< sage exr-vcr-lic-heis-curvature >}}
:::
::::

### Singlet truncations

Every consistent truncation met so far keeps the fields that are invariant under a symmetry. The theorem states the
general principle; its proof is a one-line representation-theory argument, given after the statement, and the sources
use it in this form [@duff2025, Sec. 7; @cvetic2000, Sec. 8; @hull2005, Sec. 2.2].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-vcr-singlet-consistency}
#### Singlet truncations are consistent

Let a field theory be invariant under a compact group $K$ acting linearly on its fields, and split the fields into the
$K$-invariant part $\Phi_s$ (the singlets) and the rest $\Phi_n$. Then setting $\Phi_n = 0$ solves the field
equations of $\Phi_n$ identically for every configuration of $\Phi_s$, and the remaining equations are those of the
action restricted to the singlets. Hence the truncation to all $K$-singlets is consistent. Indeed, at
$\Phi_n = 0$ the variation $\delta S/\delta\Phi_n$ is a $K$-covariant expression built from singlets only, so it is an
invariant vector of a representation without invariant vectors, hence zero.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The circle is the first case of the theorem. The example identifies $K$ and the singlets, and recovers the consistency
of the zero-mode truncation of Part III.

::: {#exm-vcr-singlet-circle}
#### The circle and the torus

On $S^1$, $K = U(1)$ acts on the mode $\phi_n$ by $e^{in\epsilon/R}$, the singlets are the zero modes, and
@def-zero-mode-truncation is the singlet truncation. On $T^n$, $K = U(1)^n$ and the singlets are the fields of
@def-vcr-torus-reduction. With a Scherk-Schwarz twist $K$ is the translation combined with the compensating symmetry,
and its singlets are the $n = 0$ modes of @prp-vcr-twisted-spectrum [@duff2025, Sec. 7].
:::

On a group manifold the relevant group is $G_L$, which acts transitively. The example shows why transitivity makes the
set of singlets finite, which is what turns the truncation into a reduction.

::: {#exm-vcr-singlet-group}
#### The group manifold

On $G$ take $K = G_L$. A $G_L$-invariant tensor is determined by its value at the identity, because $G_L$ moves the
identity to every point; the invariant metrics are the $g_{ab}\sigma^a\sigma^b$ with constant $g_{ab}$, finitely many
fields. The gauge fields of $G_R$ are $G_L$-singlets because left and right translations commute, so the truncation of
@def-vcr-group-manifold-reduction is consistent; the curvature of @prp-vcr-left-invariant-curvature is constant for the
same reason [@duff2025, Sec. 7; @hull2005, Sec. 2.2].
:::

The sphere is where the theorem has nothing to say. The example explains why no symmetry protects the non-abelian
ansatz of Part IV, which is the consistency problem stated in @def-consistency-problem.

::: {#exm-vcr-singlet-pauli}
#### Pauli's sphere

On $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$ the isometries commuting with $SO(3)$ form $N(SO(2))/SO(2) = \mathbb{Z}_2$, so there is no
continuous group whose singlets include the $SO(3)$ gauge fields: they transform in the adjoint of the isometry group
itself. The ansatz therefore keeps non-singlets, and products of the retained gauge fields source the massive spin-two
modes; Pauli observed this for six-dimensional gravity on $S^2$ in 1953 [@duff2025, Sec. 7]. The role of the Killing
vectors in such consistency questions is analysed in @hoxha2000. The symptom is the
$y$-dependence of $K_a \cdot K_b$ in @fig-vcr-group-manifold and of $\hat R$ in @exm-consistency-sphere-fails.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise makes the theorem concrete on a model with two fields. It compares an invariant potential with one
that breaks the symmetry by a single term.

::: {#exr-vcr-singlet-toy}
#### A two-field model

Let $s$ be invariant and $t \to -t$ under $\mathbb{Z}_2$. With Sage, check that $\partial V/\partial t$ vanishes at
$t = 0$ for the general invariant quartic potential, and that a term $g\,s^2t$ spoils this. Then list the $U(1)$-invariant
cubic couplings among circle modes $\phi_{-2}, \dots, \phi_2$ and check that none is linear in a massive mode with two
zero modes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every invariant monomial contains $t$ to an even power, so its $t$-derivative vanishes at $t = 0$; the term $gs^2t$ gives
the source $gs^2$. On the circle a coupling $\phi_a\phi_b\phi_c$ is invariant only if $a + b + c = 0$, which excludes
$\phi_0\phi_0\phi_n$ with $n \neq 0$:

{{< sage exr-vcr-singlet-toy >}}
:::

The theorem requires keeping all the singlets. The second exercise shows what goes wrong when one of them is dropped,
in the most familiar example.

::: {#exr-vcr-singlet-dilaton}
#### Dropping the dilaton

In the circle reduction the dilaton $\phi$ of @def-kk-ansatz is a $U(1)$ singlet. Using the reduced curvature
$\hat R = R + \tfrac14\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - 2\phi^{-1}\Box\phi$ of @sec-conventions-indices, show that setting
$\phi = 1$ is inconsistent unless $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The reduced Lagrangian is $\sqrt{-g}\,\phi\hat R = \sqrt{-g}(\phi R + \tfrac14\phi^3F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) +
\text{total derivative}$, so the $\phi$ equation is $R + \tfrac34\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 0$. At $\phi = 1$ the
remaining equations are those of Einstein-Maxwell theory, whose Maxwell stress tensor is traceless, so $R = 0$, and the
$\phi$ equation becomes the constraint $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 0$, which generic Maxwell solutions violate. The truncation to Einstein-Maxwell is inconsistent even
though the dilaton is a singlet: the theorem allows keeping all singlets, not a subset [@duff2025, Sec. 7].
:::

Truncating to a finite set of massive modes is the other tempting mistake. The last exercise shows why it fails on the
circle, by charge conservation.

::: {#exr-vcr-singlet-massive}
#### Keeping one massive level

Suppose one keeps the zero modes and the modes $n = \pm1$ of a circle reduction with a cubic interaction. Show that the
coupling $\phi_1\phi_1\phi_{-2}$ makes the truncation inconsistent, and explain why no symmetry can rescue it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The equation of $\phi_{-2}$ contains $\phi_1\phi_1$, a source built from kept modes, so $\phi_{-2} = 0$ is not a
solution once $\phi_1 \neq 0$. A symmetry protecting the truncation would have to leave $\phi_{\pm1}$ invariant and act
non-trivially on $\phi_{\pm2}$; but the charge $n$ of $\phi_1\phi_1$ is $2$, so any such symmetry would act on
$\phi_{\pm2}$ as on $\phi_1^2$, trivially. This is the statement of @def-zero-mode-truncation that finite massive
truncations are inconsistent.
:::
::::

## Sphere reductions in supergravity {#sec-vi-sphere-supergravity}

The singlet theorem explains the tori and the group manifolds, and it says nothing about spheres: their isometry group
acts on the gauge fields one wants to keep. Yet the most important reductions of supergravity are on spheres. Eleven-
dimensional supergravity has a solution $AdS_4 \times S^7$ in which a four-form flux curves both factors, and its
reduction keeping the $SO(8)$ gauge fields of $S^7$ is consistent, by cancellations that no symmetry of the original
formulation explains. This section checks the Freund-Rubin solution on its explicit metric, outlines the three
consistent sphere truncations of supergravity, and solves the numerical conditions that single them out; the last
subsection describes in one paragraph the exceptional field theory in which these truncations become generalised
Scherk-Schwarz reductions. The figure shows the radii of the Freund-Rubin vacua; the interactive version draws the two
radii to scale as the flux varies.

![Left: the radii of $AdS_4 \times S^7$ supported by the flux $F = 3m\,\epsilon$ against $m$: the seven-sphere has
radius $a = 1/m$, twice the anti-de Sitter radius $L = 1/2m$, for every value of the flux. Right: the ratio $a/L = (q -
1)/(p - 1)$ for Freund-Rubin vacua $AdS_p \times S^q$ supported by a $p$-form flux; the three maximally supersymmetric
vacua of string and M-theory are in green. Generated by `figures/vcr_freund_rubin.sage`.](figures/vcr_freund_rubin.svg){#fig-vcr-freund-rubin
width=95%}

{{< interactive vcr_freund_rubin 460 >}}

### Spontaneous compactification

In the reductions of the previous sections the product form of spacetime was imposed. In supergravity it can instead
be a solution of the field equations, selected by the dynamics, with the curvature of the compact factor balanced by
the energy of a form field. The definition names such solutions, following the review of Duff, Nilsson and Pope.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcr-spontaneous-compactification}
#### Spontaneous compactification

A **spontaneous compactification** is a solution of the higher-dimensional field equations of product form $M_d \times
X$, with $M_d$ maximally symmetric (Minkowski, de Sitter or anti-de Sitter) and $X$ compact, in which the curvature of
$X$ is supported by the fields of the theory rather than imposed [@duff2025, Sec. 2]. It is of **Freund-Rubin type**
if a $p$-form field strength is proportional to the volume form of a $p$-dimensional factor: $F = c\,\epsilon_p$ on
$M_p$ (electric) or on $X$ (magnetic). The isometry group of $X$ becomes the gauge group of the massless vectors and the
inverse radius sets the gauge coupling, $e^2 \sim Gm^2$, and the cosmological constant, $\Lambda \sim -m^2$ [@duff2025,
eqs. 1-3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The four-form of eleven-dimensional supergravity can fill the four dimensions of spacetime. This is the solution of
@def-freund-rubin-ansatz, recalled here as the first example of the definition.

::: {#exm-vcr-sc-freund-rubin}
#### $AdS_4 \times S^7$

With $F_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 3m\,\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ the field equations give $R_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$
and $R_{mn} = -6m^2g_{mn}$ in our signature (@prp-freund-rubin), so spacetime is $AdS_4$ of radius $L = 1/2m$, with
$\Lambda = -12m^2$, and $X$ is an Einstein space of positive curvature, the round $S^7$ of radius $a = 1/m$ in the most
symmetric case (@exm-freund-rubin-s7). The isometry group $SO(8)$ gives $28$ massless gauge fields.
:::

The same four-form can instead thread a four-sphere. Exchanging the roles of the factors exchanges the radii, as the
general formula of @prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry shows.

::: {#exm-vcr-sc-ads7}
#### $AdS_7 \times S^4$

A magnetic four-form $F = c\,\epsilon_4$ on $S^4$ is, after Hodge duality, an electric seven-form on $AdS_7$: $p = 7$,
$q = 4$. The ratio $a/L = (q - 1)/(p - 1) = \tfrac12$ makes the sphere half as large as the anti-de Sitter radius, the
reverse of $AdS_4 \times S^7$. The isometries $SO(5)$ give the gauge group of seven-dimensional gauged supergravity.
:::

Type IIB supergravity has a self-dual five-form, which must be electric and magnetic at once. The example is the
vacuum of the AdS/CFT correspondence, with equal radii.

::: {#exm-vcr-sc-ads5}
#### $AdS_5 \times S^5$

The self-dual five-form of type IIB supergravity takes the form $F_5 = c(\epsilon_{AdS_5} + \epsilon_{S^5})$, and both
factors feel the same flux: $p = q = 5$ and $a = L$. The isometry group $SO(6)$ of $S^5$ is the $SU(4)$ $R$-symmetry of
the dual four-dimensional gauge theory, and it gives the $15$ gauge fields of five-dimensional $N = 8$ gauged
supergravity [@hohm2014, Sec. 4.3].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The relations quoted in the definition put the scales of the four-dimensional theory together. The first exercise
combines them and draws the phenomenological conclusion of the Kaluza-Klein supergravity programme.

::: {#exr-vcr-sc-lambda}
#### The cosmological constant problem of Freund-Rubin

With $L = 1/2m$ and $\Lambda = -3/L^2$, show $\Lambda = -12m^2$. Using $e^2 \sim Gm^2$, show that $G\Lambda \sim -e^2$,
and explain why a gauge coupling of order one forces a cosmological constant of Planck size [@duff2025, Sec. 2].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-3/L^2 = -3 \cdot 4m^2 = -12m^2$. Then $G\Lambda \sim -Gm^2 \sim -e^2$: in Planck units the cosmological constant is
minus the square of the gauge coupling. For $e \sim 1$ this makes $|\Lambda|$ of the order of the Planck scale, some
$120$ orders of magnitude above the observed value; together with the absence of chiral fermions, a general obstruction for Kaluza-Klein theories on
smooth internal spaces [@Witten:1983ux], this is why
Freund-Rubin compactifications were abandoned as realistic models until the AdS/CFT correspondence gave them a new role
[@duff2025, Sec. 7].
:::

The ratio of radii holds for any Freund-Rubin vacuum. The second exercise tabulates it in Sage from the trace-reversed
Einstein equation, for the cases of the figure and two others.

::: {#exr-vcr-sc-radii}
#### Radii of Freund-Rubin vacua

With Sage, compute $L$, $a$ and $a/L$ for $AdS_p \times S^q$ with flux $c\,\epsilon_p$, using the curvatures of
@prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry, for $(p, q) = (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 7), (5, 5), (7, 4), (2, 3), (3, 7)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The ratio $a/L = (q - 1)/(p - 1)$ does not depend on $c$; $AdS_2 \times S^2$ (the Bertotti-Robinson throat of an extremal
Reissner-Nordström black hole) and $AdS_3 \times S^3$ have equal radii:

{{< sage exr-vcr-sc-radii >}}
:::

Without a form field there is nothing to balance the curvature of the sphere. The last exercise shows that pure gravity
has no product vacuum with a sphere, which is the second half of @def-consistency-problem.

::: {#exr-vcr-sc-no-flux}
#### No sphere without flux

Show that $M_4 \times S^n$ with a product metric cannot solve the vacuum Einstein equations $\hat R_{MN} = 0$, nor
$\hat R_{MN} = \hat\Lambda\hat g_{MN}$ with $M_4$ flat. Which choice of $M_4$ and $\hat\Lambda$ does allow a product
solution with $S^n$, and why is it not a Freund-Rubin solution?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a product the Ricci tensor is block diagonal with $\hat R_{mn}$ the Ricci tensor of $S^n$, $(n - 1)/a^2$ times the
positive-definite metric, which is never zero. With $\hat R_{MN} = \hat\Lambda\hat g_{MN}$ both blocks must have the same
Einstein constant, so $M_4$ must be curved like the sphere: de Sitter space, with a cosmological constant that is positive in the
physical sense and a curvature scale tied to the radius of the sphere. That is a solution with a cosmological constant rather than a flux, and its scales are tied by
$\hat\Lambda$ alone.
:::
::::

### The Freund-Rubin solution on explicit metrics

The curvatures of @prp-freund-rubin were obtained there by solving the field equations algebraically for $R_{\mu\nu}$
and $R_{mn}$. The proposition below goes the other way: it takes explicit metrics for the two factors, computes their
Ricci tensors from the Christoffel symbols, and checks that the eleven-dimensional equations hold component by
component.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry}
#### $AdS_4 \times S^7$ solves the field equations

In the signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$, the metric
$$
d\hat s^2 = \frac{L^2}{z^2}\left(dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2\right) - a^2\,d\Omega_7^2, \qquad L = \frac{1}{2m}, \quad a
= \frac1m ,
$$ {#eq-vcr-ads4-s7}
with $d\Omega_7^2$ the unit round metric in hyperspherical angles, and the flux $F_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 3m\sqrt{|g|}\,
\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ on $AdS_4$, with $\varepsilon_{0123} = 1$ the Levi-Civita symbol, satisfy $R_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R_{mn} = -6m^2g_{mn}$, $R = 6m^2$,
$F_{\mu PQR}F_\nu{}^{PQR} = -54m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $F^2 = -216m^2$, the Einstein equations $R_{MN} - \tfrac12g_{MN}R = -
\tfrac13(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR} - \tfrac18g_{MN}F^2)$ in every component, and $d{*F} + F \wedge F = 0$. For $AdS_p
\times S^q$ with a $p$-form flux $c\,\epsilon_p$ the Einstein equations give the radii ratio $a/L = (q - 1)/(p - 1)$.
The field equations are those of @prp-freund-rubin, converted from @duff2025 [eq. 7] to our signature.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation with SageManifolds in `figures/vcr_freund_rubin.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Poincaré coordinates cover half of anti-de Sitter space with a metric conformal to Minkowski space. The first example
records its curvature in our signature, where anti-de Sitter has a positive multiple of the metric as Ricci tensor.

::: {#exm-vcr-frg-poincare}
#### Poincaré $AdS_4$

The metric $\frac{L^2}{z^2}(dt^2 - d\vec x^2 - dz^2)$, $z > 0$, has $R_{\mu\nu} = \frac{3}{L^2}g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R =
\frac{12}{L^2}$ in the signature $(+, -, -, -)$; in the mostly-plus signature the same tensor reads $R_{\mu\nu} =
-\frac{3}{L^2}g_{\mu\nu}$, since $R_{\mu\nu}$ is unchanged and $g_{\mu\nu}$ flips sign (@sec-conventions-indices). With
$L = 1/2m$ this is $12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, the spacetime half of the proposition.
:::

The seven-sphere in hyperspherical angles has a diagonal metric whose components are products of sines. The example
writes it and its Ricci tensor, and checks the scaling with the radius.

::: {#exm-vcr-frg-s7}
#### The round $S^7$

In angles $\chi_0, \dots, \chi_6$ the unit metric is $d\chi_0^2 + \sin^2\chi_0\,d\chi_1^2 + \sin^2\chi_0\sin^2\chi_1\,
d\chi_2^2 + \dots$, and the sphere of radius $a$ has $R_{mn} = \frac6{a^2}\gamma_{mn}$ for its positive-definite metric
$\gamma = a^2d\Omega_7^2$ (@exr-vcr-frg-s4 for $n \leq 5$). In the book's signature $h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$, so $R_{mn} = -
\frac{6}{a^2}h_{mn} = -6m^2h_{mn}$ for $a = 1/m$.
:::

The volume of the internal space converts the eleven-dimensional Newton constant into the four-dimensional one. The
example computes it for the seven-sphere, which fixes the relation between the flux and the Planck scale.

::: {#exm-vcr-frg-newton}
#### Newton's constant in four dimensions

The unit $S^7$ has volume $\pi^4/3$, so the sphere of radius $a = 1/m$ has $\operatorname{Vol}(S^7) = \pi^4/(3m^7)$, and
reducing $\frac{1}{16\pi G_{11}}\int\sqrt{|g_{11}|}\,R$ gives $G_4 = G_{11}/\operatorname{Vol}(S^7) = 3m^7G_{11}/\pi^4$.
Four-dimensional gravity is weak at the compactification scale, $G_4m^2 = 3G_{11}m^9/\pi^4 \ll 1$, only if the
sphere is large in eleven-dimensional Planck units.
:::

Both factors of the vacuum are quadrics in flat spaces, and the explicit metrics of the proposition are charts on them.
The last example describes the vacuum this way, which makes its symmetries visible without solving any Killing
equation.

::: {#exm-vcr-frg-quadric}
#### Both factors as quadrics

The seven-sphere of radius $a$ is the quadric $\sum_{i=1}^8(Y^i)^2 = a^2$ in $\mathbb{R}^8$, and $AdS_4$ of radius $L$ is the quadric
$(X^0)^2 + (X^4)^2 - (X^1)^2 - (X^2)^2 - (X^3)^2 = L^2$ in the flat space with two time directions $X^0, X^4$, of which
@exm-grb-ads-global is the case $L = 1$ [@boskoff2024journey, Secs. 11.2 and 12.5]. The linear maps that preserve the two
quadratic forms preserve the quadrics, so the vacuum has the isometry group $SO(2, 3) \times SO(8)$, with $10 + 28 = 38$
Killing vectors: $10 = 4 \cdot 5/2$ is the maximum in four dimensions (@def-maximally-symmetric), and $SO(2, 3)$ plays for
$AdS_4$ the role of the Poincaré group, which has the same dimension. The Poincaré coordinates of @eq-vcr-ads4-s7 cover only half
of the quadric (@exm-grb-ads-global gives global coordinates), and the $28$ Killing vectors of $S^7$ give the gauge
fields of @exm-vcr-sc-freund-rubin.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Taking the trace of the Einstein equation determines the curvature scalar directly. The first exercise does this by
hand and recovers the two Ricci tensors from it.

::: {#exr-vcr-frg-trace}
#### The trace

Contract the field equation of @prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry with $g^{MN}$ in eleven dimensions to get $R = 6m^2$ from
$F^2 = -216m^2$, and then solve for $R_{\mu\nu}$ and $R_{mn}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace gives $R - \tfrac{11}2R = -\tfrac13(F^2 - \tfrac{11}8F^2)$, that is, $-\tfrac92R = \tfrac18F^2 = -27m^2$, so
$R = 6m^2$. Then $R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R - \tfrac13(-54m^2g_{\mu\nu} + 27m^2g_{\mu\nu}) = (3 + 9)m^2g_{\mu\nu}$
and $R_{mn} = 3m^2g_{mn} - \tfrac13 \cdot 27m^2g_{mn} = -6m^2g_{mn}$, since $F$ has no internal components.
:::

The same check works for every sphere, and SageManifolds computes the Ricci tensor of the round $S^n$ quickly for small
$n$. The second exercise asks for the Einstein property and the curvature scalar.

::: {#exr-vcr-frg-s4}
#### Round spheres are Einstein

With SageManifolds, show that the round $S^n$ of radius $a$ in hyperspherical angles has $R_{mn} = \frac{n - 1}{a^2}
\gamma_{mn}$ and $R = \frac{n(n - 1)}{a^2}$ for $n = 2, \dots, 5$, and deduce the curvature of the $S^4$ of $AdS_7
\times S^4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The computation confirms the Einstein property (@def-einstein-metric) for each $n$:

{{< sage exr-vcr-frg-s4 >}}

For $S^4$, $R_{mn} = 3a^{-2}\gamma_{mn}$; with $a = L/2$ from @exm-vcr-sc-ads7 the sphere is more strongly curved than
$AdS_7$, whose Ricci tensor has $6/L^2$.
:::

Reversing the orientation of the internal space flips the sign of $m$ relative to the volume form. The third exercise
shows that the bosonic solution does not see this, while supersymmetry does.

::: {#exr-vcr-frg-skew}
#### Skew-whiffing

Show that the bosonic field equations of @prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry are invariant under $m \to -m$. Using the
statement of @duff2025 [Sec. 3] that the Killing-spinor integrability condition is unchanged under orientation reversal,
explain why, apart from the round $S^7$, at most one orientation of a seven-manifold gives a supersymmetric vacuum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$m$ enters the Einstein equations only through $F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR}$ and $F^2$, quadratic in $m$, and $F \wedge F = 0$;
so $m \to -m$ maps solutions to solutions. Supersymmetry needs Killing spinors, solutions of $\tilde D_m\eta = (D_m -
\tfrac12m\Gamma_m)\eta = 0$ [@duff2025, eq. 13], which are sensitive to the sign of $m$. Reversing the orientation is
equivalent to $m \to -m$; the integrability condition is the same, but the solutions of the first-order equation differ,
and only the round sphere has Killing spinors for both signs. The other orientation, the skew-whiffed vacuum, is
non-supersymmetric but classically stable [@duff2025, Sec. 3].
:::

The quadric of @exm-vcr-frg-quadric gives global coordinates on the anti-de Sitter factor, in which the time is an
angle. The fourth exercise derives the induced metric from the embedding and checks that its curvature is the one of the
Poincaré chart.

::: {#exr-vcr-frg-global}
#### Global coordinates with Sage

Pull back the flat metric $(dX^0)^2 + (dX^4)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^3(dX^i)^2$ along $X^0 = L\cosh\rho\cos\tau$, $X^4 =
L\cosh\rho\sin\tau$, $X^i = L\sinh\rho\,n^i(\theta, \varphi)$, with $n$ the unit vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$. With Sage, check
that the image lies on the quadric, compute the induced metric and its Ricci tensor, and compare with @exm-vcr-frg-poincare.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The induced metric is $L^2(\cosh^2\rho\,d\tau^2 - d\rho^2 - \sinh^2\rho\,d\Omega_2^2)$, the metric of @exm-grb-ads-global
with radius $L$, and $R_{\mu\nu} = 3L^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = 12/L^2$, the values of the Poincaré chart:

{{< sage exr-vcr-frg-global >}}

With $L = 1/2m$ this is $R_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, the spacetime half of @prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry. The two
charts describe the same space, so the field equations hold on the whole quadric (and on its universal cover, in which
$\tau \in \mathbb{R}$), not only on the half that the Poincaré coordinates reach.
:::
::::

### Consistent sphere truncations

A Kaluza-Klein reduction on a sphere that keeps all the gauge fields of its isometry group is not a singlet truncation,
and in a generic theory it is inconsistent. In three supergravities it is nevertheless consistent, with an ansatz in
which the internal metric and the form fields depend on the scalars and on the sphere coordinates in an intricate way.
The definition names the notion; its existence in each case is quoted, not proved.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcr-consistent-sphere-truncation}
#### Consistent sphere truncation

A **consistent sphere truncation** of a theory on $M_d \times S^n$ is a reduction ansatz that keeps finitely many
$d$-dimensional fields, among them the gauge fields of the full isometry group $SO(n + 1)$, such that every solution of
the $d$-dimensional equations lifts to a solution of the higher-dimensional ones: all dependence on the sphere
coordinates cancels from the field equations [@cvetic2000, Sec. 1; @duff2025, Sec. 7]. The three supergravity cases are
eleven-dimensional supergravity on $S^7$, giving $N = 8$ supergravity in four dimensions with gauge group $SO(8)$,
$28$ vectors and $70$ scalars; eleven-dimensional supergravity on $S^4$, giving $SO(5)$ gauged supergravity in seven
dimensions; and type IIB supergravity on $S^5$, giving $SO(6)$ gauged supergravity in five dimensions [@cvetic2000,
Table 1; @hohm2014, Sec. 4]. All massless fields must be kept, including those that the gauge fields source, such as
the $35$ pseudoscalars of $S^7$ [@cvetic2000, Sec. 1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The seven-sphere case has a long history, recalled in the review of Duff, Nilsson and Pope. The example summarises it,
because the length of that history measures how unexpected the consistency is.

::: {#exm-vcr-cst-s7}
#### The seven-sphere

The truncation of eleven-dimensional supergravity on $S^7$ to $SO(8)$ gauged $N = 8$ supergravity was conjectured in
1982; in 1984 the source of the massive spin-two modes built from two $SO(8)$ Yang-Mills fields, the term that kills
Pauli's sphere (@exm-vcr-singlet-pauli), was found to cancel between the metric and the four-form contributions; de Wit
and Nicolai gave the full ansatz and argument in 1987, and the last gaps in the four-form ansatz were closed in 2012
[@duff2025, Sec. 7].
:::

Pure gravity is the case that fails, and the obstruction can be seen before any computation on the sphere. The
example gives the group-theoretical argument of Cvetič, Lü and Pope.

::: {#exm-vcr-cst-pure-gravity}
#### Why pure gravity fails

Reducing first on the torus $T^n$, pure gravity gives scalars in $GL(n, \mathbb{R})/SO(n)$, whose compact symmetry is
$SO(n)$. A consistent $S^n$ reduction keeping $SO(n + 1)$ gauge fields would gauge $SO(n + 1)$ inside the global symmetry
of this scalar manifold, which needs the compact subgroup to contain $SO(n + 1)$; it does not, so "it is not possible to
perform a consistent $n$-sphere reduction of a pure gravity theory, in which the Yang-Mills fields of $SO(n + 1)$ are
retained" [@cvetic2000, Sec. 1]. The criterion proves inconsistency; it does not by itself prove consistency where it
is met [@cvetic2000, Sec. 8].
:::

Between the generic failure and the three supergravity cases there is a family that works in every dimension. The
example describes it, together with its truncation to the $SU(2)$ group manifold.

::: {#exm-vcr-cst-s3}
#### Three-spheres with a three-form

Gravity coupled to a dilaton and a three-form field strength with the string coupling, $\mathcal{L} = R - \tfrac12(\partial
\phi)^2 - \tfrac1{12}e^{-a\phi}F_3^2$ in their conventions, admits a consistent $S^3$ reduction keeping all $SO(4)$ gauge
fields in any dimension $D$ [@cvetic2000, Sec. 3]. Keeping only $SU(2)_L$ singlets gives a truncation whose consistency
is "no longer anything surprising": it is the group-manifold reduction on $SU(2)$, a singlet truncation, and its scalars
describe homogeneous deformations of $S^3$ only [@cvetic2000, Sec. 4.1].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The field content of the three truncations can be counted from group theory. The first exercise does so in Sage,
including the split of the $70$ scalars of $N = 8$ supergravity.

::: {#exr-vcr-cst-count}
#### Counting the fields

Compute the number of gauge fields of the $S^4$, $S^5$ and $S^7$ truncations, and show with Sage that the Hodge star
on four-forms of $\mathbb{R}^8$ has eigenvalues $\pm1$ with multiplicity $35$ each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dim SO(5) = 10$, $\dim SO(6) = 15$, $\dim SO(8) = 28$. The $70 = \binom84$ scalars of $N = 8$ supergravity sit in the
four-forms of $SO(8)$, which split into $35$ self-dual (scalars) and $35$ anti-self-dual (pseudoscalars), matching
$\dim E_7 - \dim SU(8) = 70$ of @exr-vcr-torus-e7:

{{< sage exr-vcr-cst-count >}}
:::

The argument of @exm-vcr-cst-pure-gravity rests on a statement about compact subgroups. The second exercise proves the
dimension count behind it.

::: {#exr-vcr-cst-gl}
#### Compact subgroups of $GL(n)$

Show that the maximal compact subgroup of $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ is $O(n)$, of dimension $\tfrac12n(n - 1)$, and that
$SO(n + 1)$, of dimension $\tfrac12n(n + 1)$, cannot be a subgroup of it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A compact subgroup preserves a positive-definite inner product (average any inner product over the group with its Haar
measure), so it is conjugate to a subgroup of $O(n)$. Since $\tfrac12n(n + 1) > \tfrac12n(n - 1)$, $SO(n + 1)$ has
larger dimension than $O(n)$ and cannot embed in it. The scalars of the torus-reduced pure gravity are therefore too few
to be acted on by $SO(n + 1)$ in the required way, and the sphere reduction fails.
:::

The two truncations of @exm-vcr-cst-s3 differ in how much of the isometry group they keep. The last exercise explains
the difference with the singlet theorem.

::: {#exr-vcr-cst-singlet}
#### $SO(4)$ against $SU(2)_L$

The isometry group of $S^3 = SU(2)$ is $SO(4) = (SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R)/\mathbb{Z}_2$. Explain why the truncation
keeping only the $SU(2)_R$ gauge fields and the $SU(2)_L$ singlets is consistent by @thm-vcr-singlet-consistency, and
why keeping all six $SO(4)$ gauge fields is not covered by the theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $SU(2)_R$ gauge fields and the left-invariant metrics are $SU(2)_L$-invariant (@exm-vcr-singlet-group), and $SU(2)_L$
is compact, so the theorem applies. With all of $SO(4)$ kept there is no continuous isometry left that commutes with
$SO(4)$ and leaves every kept field invariant: the $SU(2)_L$ gauge fields transform under $SU(2)_L$ itself. Consistency of
the $SO(4)$ truncation therefore needs the special three-form coupling of @exm-vcr-cst-s3, verified by direct
computation in @cvetic2000 [Sec. 3].
:::
::::

### Where consistent sphere truncations exist

The three supergravity cases are not accidents, and two different arguments single them out. Cvetič, Lü and Pope ask
when gravity with a $p$-form, reduced on a torus, has a scalar manifold large enough to contain the sphere isometry
group, and find a numerical condition on the dimension $D$ and the degree $p$. Hohm and Samtleben reformulate the
supergravities as **exceptional field theories**: the internal coordinates are enlarged to a representation of the
exceptional group $E_{d(d)}$ (the $56$ of $E_{7(7)}$ in the four-dimensional case), the fields are reorganised into
$E_{d(d)}$-covariant objects subject to a section condition that removes the extra coordinates, and the sphere
truncations become generalised Scherk-Schwarz reductions $\mathcal{M}_{MN}(x, Y) = U_M{}^K(Y)U_N{}^L(Y)M_{KL}(x)$
with a twist matrix $U$ whose consistency conditions say that a certain combination of $U^{-1}\partial U$ is constant
[@hohm2014, eqs. 1.1-1.2]. In that formulation the consistency of the sphere truncations is manifest, the analogue of the
singlet argument for the enlarged symmetry [@duff2025, Sec. 7], and the sphere solutions exist exactly when another
numerical relation holds. The proposition solves both relations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcr-sphere-criterion}
#### The numerical conditions

(i) The condition $2D - 4 = (p - 1)(D - p - 1)$ for gravity with a $p$-form and no dilaton to have the symmetry
enhancement needed for a consistent sphere reduction [@cvetic2000, eq. 2] has, for $p \geq 2$ and $D \geq p + 2$,
exactly the solutions $(D, p) = (11, 4), (10, 5), (11, 7)$. (ii) With a dilaton, the required coupling $a^2 = 4 - 2(p -
1)(D - p - 1)/(D - 2)$ [@cvetic2000, eq. 4] equals $2(D - 1)/(D - 2)$ for $p = 2$ and $8/(D - 2)$ for $p = 3$,
positive in every dimension. (iii) The relation $\tfrac12(D - 1) = (n - 2)/(n - 4)$ of the $SL(n)$ twist matrices
[@hohm2014, eq. 1.6] has, for $n > 4$, exactly the solutions $(D, n) = (7, 5), (5, 6), (4, 8)$. That the
relations characterise the consistent truncations is quoted from the sources.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** The solutions of the relations are checked by exact computation in `figures/vcr_freund_rubin.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first solution is eleven-dimensional supergravity, whose four-form gives both the $S^7$ and, by duality, the $S^4$
reduction. The example checks the arithmetic and matches the two solutions with $p = 4$ and $p = 7$.

::: {#exm-vcr-crit-11}
#### Eleven dimensions

For $D = 11$, $p = 4$: $2 \cdot 11 - 4 = 18 = 3 \cdot 6$; for $p = 7$: $18 = 6 \cdot 3$. The four-form and its dual
seven-form are the two descriptions of the same field, and the two solutions correspond to the reductions on $S^7$
(electric four-form on $AdS_4$) and on $S^4$ (magnetic four-form on the sphere), the $(4, 7)$ and $(7, 4)$ of
@fig-vcr-freund-rubin.
:::

The second solution is type IIB supergravity, the only one with a self-dual form. The example checks it and explains
why self-duality matters.

::: {#exm-vcr-crit-iib}
#### Ten dimensions

For $D = 10$, $p = 5$: $2 \cdot 10 - 4 = 16 = 4 \cdot 4$, a solution that is its own dual since $D - p = p$. The
corresponding theory is type IIB supergravity, whose five-form must be self-dual for the enhancement to occur
[@cvetic2000, Sec. 1], and the sphere is the $S^5$ of $AdS_5 \times S^5$.
:::

The relation of Hohm and Samtleben has the same three solutions in a different guise. The example matches them with
the exceptional groups and the sphere reductions.

::: {#exm-vcr-crit-hohm}
#### Twist matrices for three spheres

The solutions $(D, n) = (7, 5), (5, 6), (4, 8)$ use $SL(5)$, $SL(6) \subset E_{6(6)}$ and $SL(8) \subset E_{7(7)}$, and
the twist matrices describe the round spheres $S^{n - 1} = S^4, S^5, S^7$: these are "the dimensions of the known sphere
compactifications $AdS_D \times S^{n - 1}$" [@hohm2014, eq. 1.6 and Sec. 1]. The same twist matrices with indefinite signature give
consistent truncations on hyperboloids, with non-compact gauge groups $SO(p, q)$ [@hohm2014, Sec. 4.2].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first relation can be solved without a computer. The first exercise asks for the short argument that rules out all
other degrees.

::: {#exr-vcr-crit-solve}
#### Solving the Cvetič-Lü-Pope relation

Rewrite $2D - 4 = (p - 1)(D - p - 1)$ as $D = p + 3 + \frac{4}{p - 3}$ for $p \neq 3$, deduce that $p - 3$ divides $4$,
and list the solutions with $p \geq 2$, $D \geq p + 2$. What happens for $p = 3$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding, $2D - 4 = pD - p^2 - D + 1$, so $D(p - 3) = p^2 - 5$ and $D = (p^2 - 5)/(p - 3) = p + 3 + 4/(p - 3)$. Hence
$p - 3 \in \{\pm1, \pm2, \pm4\}$, that is, $p \in \{1, 2, 4, 5, 7, -1\}$, with $D = 2, 1, 11, 10, 11$ for the positive
values; the constraints $p \geq 2$, $D \geq p + 2$ leave $(11, 4), (10, 5), (11, 7)$. For $p = 3$ the relation reads
$2D - 4 = 2D - 8$, which has no solution; three-forms need a dilaton (@prp-vcr-sphere-criterion (ii)).
:::

The second relation yields to the same trick of dividing out the polynomial. The exercise solves it and identifies
the values of $n$ that are excluded.

::: {#exr-vcr-crit-hohm-solve}
#### Solving the Hohm-Samtleben relation

Show that $\tfrac12(D - 1) = (n - 2)/(n - 4)$ is equivalent to $D = 3 + 4/(n - 4)$ and find all solutions with $n > 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(n - 2)/(n - 4) = 1 + 2/(n - 4)$, so $D - 1 = 2 + 4/(n - 4)$ and $D = 3 + 4/(n - 4)$. An integer $D$ requires $n - 4
\mid 4$, that is, $n = 5, 6, 8$, with $D = 7, 5, 4$; for $n > 8$ the value $4/(n - 4)$ is not an integer.
:::

The dilaton coupling is symmetric under exchanging a form with its dual. The last exercise checks this in Sage and
tabulates the couplings that allow $S^2$ and $S^3$ reductions in every dimension.

::: {#exr-vcr-crit-sage}
#### The dilaton coupling

With Sage, check that $a^2(D, p) = a^2(D, D - p)$, tabulate $a^2$ for $p = 2, 3$ and $D = 4, \dots, 11$, and find the
pairs $(D, p)$ with $a^2 = 0$ for $D \leq 26$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coupling depends on $p$ only through $(p - 1)(D - p - 1)$, which is symmetric under $p \to D - p$. It vanishes
exactly at the solutions of (i): the theories that need no dilaton are the dilaton-free ones of the proposition:

{{< sage exr-vcr-crit-sage >}}
:::
::::

## Symmetric-field schemes compared {#sec-vi-symmetric-schemes}

Coset space dimensional reduction (Part V) does not truncate a Kaluza-Klein tower: it imposes that the fields be
symmetric under the isometries of the internal space up to a compensating gauge transformation, and keeps whatever
solves the constraints. The Scherk-Schwarz twist of @sec-vi-torus-scherk-schwarz is a constraint of the same kind,
with a global symmetry as compensator, and two more recent schemes follow the same pattern: the equivariant reduction
of Dolan and Szabo, in which the compensator lives on a non-trivial bundle with a monopole background, and the fuzzy
sphere, in which the internal space itself is replaced by matrices. This section defines the common notion, compares
the four schemes in a table, and works out the vacua of the equivariant and fuzzy reductions. The figure shows the
equivariant Higgs potential for three choices of the gauge group and the fuzzy spheres of increasing size.
CSDR has also been carried out with gravity in the higher-dimensional theory [@chatzistavrakidis2007eym].

![Left: the Higgs potential of the $SU(2)$-equivariant reduction with $m = 1$ over a sphere of radius $R$, along the
vacuum direction, in units $g = R = 1$, for the blocks $(k_0, k_1) = (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1)$; the minimum is at
$|\phi| = 1/(2gR)$ (dashed) with height $(k_0 - k_1)/(32g^2R^4)$. Right: fuzzy spheres: the $N$ eigenvalues of $X_3 =
J_3/\sqrt{j(j + 1)}$ in the $N$-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are $N$ latitudes of the unit sphere,
which fill it as $N$ grows. Generated by `figures/vcr_equivariant.sage`.](figures/vcr_equivariant.svg){#fig-vcr-equivariant
width=95%}

{{< interactive vcr_equivariant 460 >}}

The table compares the four schemes by what is required to be symmetric, what compensates the symmetry, what survives
in four dimensions and which example the chapter or the book works out. In every row the surviving fields are the
singlets of a combined action, which is why each truncation is consistent at least for the gauge sector on a fixed
background (@thm-vcr-singlet-consistency).

| scheme | internal space | symmetry required | compensated by | what survives | example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSDR | coset $S/R$ | $S$-isometries of all fields | gauge transformations of $G$ | gauge group $C_G(R)$, Higgs fields from matching $R$-representations, a quartic potential | $SU(3)$ over $S^2$ gives $SU(2) \times U(1)$ (Part V) |
| Scherk-Schwarz | $S^1$, or a group $G$ | translations, or $G_L$ | a global symmetry, or nothing | twisted zero modes with masses $\lvert\omega\rvert$; gauged supergravity | supersymmetry breaking at $1/2R$ (@exm-vcr-twisted-susy) |
| equivariant | $\mathbb{C}P^1 = SU(2)/U(1)$ | $SU(2)$ lifted to a bundle | bundle maps, monopoles of charges $m - 2i$ | quiver gauge theory $\prod_iU(k_i)$, bifundamental Higgs fields | $SU(3) \to SU(2) \times U(1) \to U(1)$ (@exm-vcr-eq-su3) |
| fuzzy sphere | $N \times N$ matrices | $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ acting by commutators | gauge transformations of the matrix model | broken gauge group, a finite tower of massive modes | chiral models from orbifolds (@exm-vcr-fz-vacuum) |

### Symmetric fields

The four rows of the table share one definition. It generalises @def-symmetric-gauge-field of Part V by letting the
compensating transformation be any symmetry of the higher-dimensional theory, not only a gauge transformation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcr-symmetric-field-scheme}
#### Symmetric-field reduction

Let a group $S$ act on the internal space $Y$ with generators $\xi_A$, and let the higher-dimensional theory have a
symmetry group $\mathcal{K}$ (gauge or global) acting on its fields by $\delta_W$. A field configuration $\Phi$ is
**symmetric** if every $S$-transformation of it is compensated by a $\mathcal{K}$-transformation,
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\Phi = \delta_{W_A}\Phi ,
$$ {#eq-vcr-symmetric-field}
with parameters $W_A$ on $Y$. A **symmetric-field reduction** keeps exactly the symmetric configurations; the
compatibility of @eq-vcr-symmetric-field with the algebra of the $\xi_A$ constrains the $W_A$, and the fields that solve
the constraints are the four-dimensional fields. Since the configurations solving @eq-vcr-symmetric-field are the
invariants of the combined action of $S$ and $\mathcal{K}$, the reduction is a singlet truncation in the sense of
@thm-vcr-singlet-consistency; for Yang-Mills theory on a reductive coset of a unimodular $S$ the reduced equations of
motion are those of the reduced action [@chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, Sec. 3.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Coset space dimensional reduction is the case in which the compensator is a gauge transformation. The first example
recalls it in the language of the definition.

::: {#exm-vcr-sfs-csdr}
#### CSDR

With $Y = S/R$, $\mathcal{K}$ the gauge group $G$ and $\delta_W\hat A = DW$, @eq-vcr-symmetric-field is
@eq-symmetric-field. The solution keeps the four-dimensional gauge fields commuting with the embedded $R$, so the gauge
group is the centraliser $H = C_G(R)$, and the internal components become Higgs fields for every matching pair of
$R$-representations [@manolakos2016, eqs. 5-6]; the quartic potential of @sec-csdr-potential follows.
:::

The Scherk-Schwarz twist fits the same mould with a global compensator. The example identifies the ingredients for the
circle and for a group manifold.

::: {#exm-vcr-sfs-ss}
#### Scherk-Schwarz

On $Y = S^1$, $S = U(1)$ acts by $\xi = \partial_y$ and the compensator is a global symmetry with generator $M$:
@eq-vcr-symmetric-field reads $\partial_y\Phi = M\Phi$, whose solutions are $e^{yM}\Phi_0(x)$, the ansatz of
@def-vcr-scherk-schwarz-twist. On a group manifold, with $\xi$ the generators of $G_L$ and a trivial compensator, the
condition $\mathcal{L}_\xi\Phi = 0$ selects the left-invariant fields of @def-vcr-group-manifold-reduction
[@chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, Sec. 2.2].
:::

The equivariant scheme lets the compensator act on a non-trivial bundle, so that the reduced fields carry a monopole
background. The example previews the definition of the next subsection.

::: {#exm-vcr-sfs-equivariant}
#### Equivariant reduction

On $Y = \mathbb{C}P^1 = SU(2)/U(1)$ the gauge field lives on a bundle $SU(2) \times_{U(1)} E$, and $SU(2)$ acts on it
through a representation of its $U(1)$ subgroup on the fibre. The compensator is the bundle map, and the solutions
include the monopole connections $a_p$ that an ansatz on a trivial bundle misses [@dolan2009, Sec. 1]; this is the
difference from CSDR, where "this scheme does not seem to naturally allow for the incorporation of topologically
non-trivial background fields" [@dolan2009, Sec. 1].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
With a trivial compensator the definition reduces to ordinary invariance. The first exercise asks what survives then on
a coset, which shows why CSDR needs the compensator.

::: {#exr-vcr-sfs-trivial}
#### A trivial compensator

Take $W_A = 0$ in @eq-vcr-symmetric-field for a scalar field on $S^2$ with $S = SO(3)$. Show that only constant fields
survive, and that a vector field on $S^2$ that is $SO(3)$-invariant must vanish. What does a non-zero $W_A$ add?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\phi = \xi_A\phi = 0$ for the three Killing vectors, which span the tangent space at every point,
forces $d\phi = 0$. An invariant vector field at the north pole must be fixed by the rotations about the axis, which act
on the tangent plane as $SO(2)$ with no fixed vector, so it vanishes there and, by transitivity, everywhere. A
compensator $W_A$ allows the field to rotate in the gauge group as it is moved, and if the isotropy $SO(2)$ is embedded
in $G$ the internal components can be invariant under the combined rotation: these are the CSDR Higgs fields.
:::

The second exercise rewrites the twisted circle reduction explicitly as a symmetric-field reduction. It identifies the
combined group whose singlets the reduction keeps.

::: {#exr-vcr-sfs-ss-as-symmetric}
#### The twist as a symmetry condition

Show that the finite form of $\partial_y\Phi = M\Phi$ is $\Phi(y + c) = e^{cM}\Phi(y)$ for all $c$, and that the
fields satisfying it are the invariants of the combined transformation $T_c = (\text{translation by } c) \circ
e^{-cM}$. Why does periodicity require $e^{2\pi RM}$ to be a symmetry, but not the identity?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Integrating $\partial_y\Phi = M\Phi$ gives $\Phi(y + c) = e^{cM}\Phi(y)$, that is, $e^{-cM}\Phi(y + c) = \Phi(y)$,
which says $T_c\Phi = \Phi$. The field is defined on the circle, so its values at $y$ and $y + 2\pi R$ must be related
by a transformation that leaves the Lagrangian invariant; $e^{2\pi RM}$ is such a transformation, the monodromy of
@eq-vcr-ss-twist, and it need not be trivial since the Lagrangian, not the field, must be single-valued.
:::

In CSDR the surviving gauge group is a centraliser, and centralisers are computed by linear algebra. The last exercise
computes three of them in Sage.

::: {#exr-vcr-sfs-centraliser}
#### Centralisers in Sage

With Sage, compute the dimension of the centraliser in $\mathfrak{sl}(3)$ of $\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ and of
$\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$, and in $\mathfrak{sl}(4)$ of $\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -1, -1)$, and identify the
groups.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The centraliser of a diagonal matrix consists of the block-diagonal matrices with blocks on its equal eigenvalues, with
the trace removed: dimensions $4$ ($\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$, the electroweak group of
@def-csdr-centraliser), $2$ (the Cartan subalgebra) and $7$ ($\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus
\mathfrak{u}(1)$, the $m = 1$, $k_0 = k_1 = 2$ case of @def-vcr-equivariant-reduction):

{{< sage exr-vcr-sfs-centraliser >}}
:::
::::

### Equivariant dimensional reduction

Dolan and Szabo reduce a $U(k)$ gauge theory on $M \times \mathbb{C}P^1$ by asking for $SU(2)$-equivariant gauge
fields on a bundle twisted by monopoles. The definition gives their ansatz and the reduced theory, a quiver gauge theory
whose potential breaks the symmetry dynamically.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcr-equivariant-reduction}
#### Equivariant dimensional reduction

Let $\mathbb{C}P^1 = SU(2)/U(1)$ be the sphere of radius $R$ with stereographic coordinate $y$, and fix the spin-$m/2$
representation of $SU(2)$ with multiplicities $k_0, \dots, k_m$, $\sum_ik_i = k$; its $U(1)$ weights are $p_i = m -
2i$. The **equivariant dimensional reduction** of a $U(k)$ gauge theory keeps the $SU(2)$-equivariant connections
$$
\mathcal{A} = \sum_iA^i(x) \otimes \Pi_i + \mathbb{1} \otimes \sum_ia_{p_i}(y)\,\Pi_i + \boldsymbol{\phi}(x) \otimes
\bar\beta(y) - \boldsymbol{\phi}(x)^\dagger \otimes \beta(y) ,
$$ {#eq-vcr-equivariant-ansatz}
where $\Pi_i$ projects on the block $i$, $A^i$ is a $U(k_i)$ gauge field, $a_p = \frac{p}{2(1 + y\bar y)}(\bar y\,dy -
y\,d\bar y)$ is the $SU(2)$-invariant monopole connection of charge $p$, $\beta = 2dy/(1 + y\bar y)$, and
$\boldsymbol{\phi}$ has the bifundamental Higgs fields $\phi_{i + 1}$ in the blocks $(i, i + 1)$ [@dolan2009, eqs.
2.13, 2.16-2.19]. Every $SU(2)$-invariant connection has this form up to gauge transformations [@dolan2009, Sec. 2.2].
The reduced theory is a quiver gauge theory with gauge group $\prod_iU(k_i)$ and the potential
$$
V(\boldsymbol{\phi}) = \frac{g^2}2\operatorname{tr}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{4g^2R^2} - [\boldsymbol{\phi},
\boldsymbol{\phi}^\dagger]\right)^2, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \sum_ip_i\Pi_i ,
$$ {#eq-vcr-equivariant-potential}
with the four-dimensional coupling $g^2 = \tilde g^2/4\pi R^2$ [@dolan2009, eqs. 3.5-3.7].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
With $m = 0$ the representation is trivial and there is nothing to break. The first example records this case, which is
ordinary dimensional reduction on a sphere with no flux.

::: {#exm-vcr-eq-m0}
#### $m = 0$

For the trivial representation there is one block, $p_0 = 0$, no monopole, no Higgs field, and
@eq-vcr-equivariant-ansatz is a $U(k)$ gauge field independent of $y$ with no internal components: the theory on $M$ is
pure $U(k)$ Yang-Mills with $V = 0$. Symmetry breaking needs $m \geq 1$, where the monopole charges $p_i \neq 0$ make
$\boldsymbol\Sigma$ non-zero.
:::

The smallest non-trivial case has two blocks of rank one. The example shows that it is the abelian Higgs model, with a
mass parameter set by the monopole charge.

::: {#exm-vcr-eq-abelian}
#### The abelian Higgs model

For $m = 1$, $k_0 = k_1 = 1$: $p = (1, -1)$, gauge group $U(1) \times U(1)$, one complex Higgs field $\phi$ of charge
$(1, -1)$, and @eq-vcr-equivariant-potential is $V = g^2(|\phi|^2 - \frac1{4g^2R^2})^2$, the Mexican hat of
@prp-higgs-minimum with the minimum at $|\phi| = 1/2gR$ (@prp-vcr-symmetric-vacua). The overall $U(1)$ decouples and the
relative $U(1)$ is broken by the Higgs mechanism (@def-higgs-mechanism).
:::

With blocks of ranks two and one the gauge group contains the electroweak group. The example gives the breaking pattern
and the weak mixing angle that Dolan and Szabo find, which is not the observed one.

::: {#exm-vcr-eq-su3}
#### $SU(3) \to SU(2) \times U(1) \to U(1)$

For $m = 1$, $(k_0, k_1) = (2, 1)$ the reduced gauge group is $S(U(2) \times U(1)) = SU(2) \times U(1)$, the centraliser
of @exr-vcr-sfs-centraliser, with a Higgs doublet $\phi$. The vacuum $\phi^0 = \frac{1}{2gR}\binom01$ breaks it to
$U(1)$ with $\mu_W = 1/(2\sqrt2R)$, $\mu_Z = 2\mu_W$ and $\sin^2\theta_W = \tfrac34$, "not a realistic model for
electroweak interactions" [@dolan2009, Sec. 4.1, eqs. 4.11-4.18]; the CSDR model of Part V has the same group theory.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The weights of the $SU(2)$ representation fix the monopole charges and the quiver. The first exercise lists them for a
larger representation and counts the fields.

::: {#exr-vcr-eq-charges}
#### The quiver for $m = 3$

For $m = 3$ with all $k_i = n$, list the monopole charges $p_i$, the gauge group, the Higgs fields with their
representations, and the dimension of the reduced gauge group.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p = (3, 1, -1, -3)$; gauge group $U(n)^4$ (or $U(1)^3 \times SU(n)^4$ after removing the decoupled overall $U(1)$
[@dolan2009, eq. 3.4]); three Higgs fields $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$ in the bifundamentals $(n_{i - 1}, \bar n_i)$ of
neighbouring blocks, a linear quiver with four nodes and three arrows; dimension $4n^2$. Each arrow joins blocks whose
charges differ by $2$, the charge of $\bar\beta$.
:::

A vacuum with $V = 0$ needs $\boldsymbol\Sigma/4g^2R^2$ to be a commutator. The second exercise derives the trace
condition that this imposes, which explains the vacuum energy of @exm-vcr-eq-su3.

::: {#exr-vcr-eq-trace}
#### When the vacuum energy vanishes

Show that $V = 0$ is possible only if $\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Sigma = \sum_ip_ik_i = 0$. For $m = 1$, deduce that
$k_0 = k_1$ is necessary, and explain why $(k_0, k_1) = (2, 1)$ must have a positive vacuum energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A commutator is traceless, so $V = 0$ requires $\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Sigma = 0$. For $m = 1$,
$\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Sigma = k_0 - k_1$. With $(2, 1)$ the trace is $1$, and since $V$ is the squared norm of
$\boldsymbol\Sigma/4g^2R^2 - [\boldsymbol\phi, \boldsymbol\phi^\dagger]$, whose trace part cannot be cancelled, $V
\geq \frac{g^2}{2}\frac{(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Sigma)^2}{k(4g^2R^2)^2} > 0$; the actual minimum is $1/(32g^2R^4)$
(@prp-vcr-symmetric-vacua).
:::

The monopole connections carry the topology of the scheme. The last exercise computes their curvature and flux in Sage,
and meets the orientation convention that the reading note warns about.

::: {#exr-vcr-eq-monopole}
#### The monopole connection

With $y = x_1 + ix_2$, write $a_p$ of @def-vcr-equivariant-reduction in real coordinates, compute $f_p = da_p$ with
SageManifolds, and integrate it over the plane. Compare with $f_p = -\frac{p}{(1 + y\bar y)^2}dy \wedge d\bar y$ of
@dolan2009 [eq. 2.14].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a_p = ip(x_1dx_2 - x_2dx_1)/(1 + |y|^2)$ is anti-Hermitian, $f_p = \frac{2ip}{(1 + |y|^2)^2}dx_1 \wedge dx_2$, which
equals the quoted form since $dy \wedge d\bar y = -2i\,dx_1 \wedge dx_2$, and $\int f_p = 2\pi ip$. Hence
$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int f_p = -p$ with the orientation $dx_1 \wedge dx_2$; @dolan2009 [eq. 2.15] state $+p$, which
corresponds to the opposite orientation. The magnitude $|p|$, the monopole charge, is unambiguous:

{{< sage exr-vcr-eq-monopole >}}
:::
::::

### Fuzzy spheres

A fuzzy sphere replaces the functions on $S^2$ by $N \times N$ matrices, keeping the action of $SU(2)$ but truncating
the spherical harmonics at angular momentum $N - 1$. In a four-dimensional gauge theory with three adjoint scalars such
matrices can appear as a vacuum, and the theory then behaves at intermediate energies like a gauge theory on $M_4 \times
S^2_N$ with a finite tower of massive modes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcr-fuzzy-sphere}
#### Fuzzy sphere

The **fuzzy sphere** $S^2_N$ is the algebra of $N \times N$ complex matrices with the coordinates $X_a = J_a$, the
generators of the $N$-dimensional irreducible representation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ (@sec-weights-su2), which satisfy
$$
[X_a, X_b] = i\epsilon_{abc}X_c, \qquad X_aX_a = \frac{N^2 - 1}{4}\mathbb{1} .
$$ {#eq-vcr-fuzzy}
In a gauge theory with three adjoint scalars $\phi_a$ and the potential $V = \tfrac14\operatorname{tr}F_{ab}^\dagger
F_{ab}$, $F_{ab} = [\phi_a, \phi_b] - i\epsilon_{abc}\phi_c$, the configuration $\phi_a = X_a$ (possibly $\oplus\,0$)
is a vacuum, and the fluctuations around it organise into a finite Kaluza-Klein tower on $S^2_N$: the extra dimensions
are generated dynamically, the reversed approach summarised in @chatzistavrakidis2010orb [Sec. 1]. The orbifold version uses the twisted relation
$[\phi_a, \phi_b] = i\epsilon_{abc}\phi_c^\dagger$ [@chatzistavrakidis2010orb, eqs. 14 and 29-30].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest fuzzy sphere has two points: the two eigenvalues of $J_3$ for spin one-half. The example computes its
radius, which already differs from the classical value.

::: {#exm-vcr-fz-two}
#### $N = 2$

For $N = 2$, $X_a = \tfrac12\sigma_a$ and $X_aX_a = \tfrac34\mathbb{1}$: a "sphere" of radius $\sqrt3/2$ whose
coordinate $X_3$ takes only the values $\pm\tfrac12$, the north and south poles of @fig-vcr-equivariant. The coordinates
do not commute, $[X_1, X_2] = iX_3$, so no point of the sphere can be localised: the uncertainty is of the order of the
radius.
:::

The functions on the fuzzy sphere are the matrices, and the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ action by commutators decomposes them
into angular momenta. The example shows that this is the spherical-harmonic expansion cut off at $l = N - 1$.

::: {#exm-vcr-fz-functions}
#### Fuzzy spherical harmonics

Under $X \mapsto [J_a, X]$ the $N^2$-dimensional space of matrices decomposes into spins $l = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1$, since
$N \otimes \bar N = \bigoplus_{l = 0}^{N - 1}(2l + 1)$ and $\sum_l(2l + 1) = N^2$ (@exr-vcr-fz-casimir). The Laplacian
$\sum_a[J_a, [J_a, \cdot]]$ has eigenvalues $l(l + 1)$, those of the round sphere, but only up to $l = N - 1$: a
field on $S^2_N$ has a finite Kaluza-Klein tower.
:::

Fuzzy spheres appear dynamically when the potential is a square of the fuzzy-sphere relation. The example states the
vacuum and the gauge symmetry it leaves, following the orbifold models of Chatzistavrakidis, Steinacker and Zoupanos.

::: {#exm-vcr-fz-vacuum}
#### A dynamical fuzzy sphere

With $\phi_a$ in the adjoint of $SU(N)$ the potential of the definition vanishes exactly when $\phi_a$ satisfies
the relations @eq-vcr-fuzzy, for instance $\phi_a = J_a^{(N - n)} \oplus 0_n$, which breaks $SU(N)$ to $SU(n) \times
U(1)$ (@exr-vcr-fz-schur). In the orbifold models the twisted analogue $\phi^i = \Omega(\mathbb{1}_3 \otimes
(\lambda^i_{(N - n)} \oplus 0_n))$ breaks $SU(N)^3$ to $SU(n)^3$ and is interpreted as $\mathbb{R}^4 \times \tilde
S^2_N$ [@chatzistavrakidis2010orb, eq. 33]. In the $\mathbb{Z}_3$ orbifold of $N = 4$
super Yang-Mills the twisted version of this vacuum gives chiral fermions and three families, which earlier fuzzy
reductions could not [@chatzistavrakidis2010orb, Secs. 1 and 4].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The decomposition of the matrices into angular momenta can be computed directly. The first exercise does this in Sage
for small $N$, together with the Casimir.

::: {#exr-vcr-fz-casimir}
#### The fuzzy Laplacian in Sage

With Sage, build $J_a$ for $N = 2, 3, 4$, check $J_aJ_a = \frac{N^2 - 1}4$, and compute the eigenvalues and multiplicities
of $C(X) = \sum_a[J_a, [J_a, X]]$ on the $N \times N$ matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues are $l(l + 1)$ with multiplicity $2l + 1$ for $l = 0, \dots, N - 1$:

{{< sage exr-vcr-fz-casimir >}}
:::

The fuzzy sphere becomes commutative as $N$ grows, which is what justifies calling it a sphere. The second exercise
measures the non-commutativity at fixed radius.

::: {#exr-vcr-fz-limit}
#### The commutative limit

Normalise $x_a = X_a/\sqrt{j(j + 1)}$ with $N = 2j + 1$, so that $x_ax_a = \mathbb{1}$. Show that $[x_a, x_b] =
i\epsilon_{abc}x_c/\sqrt{j(j + 1)}$ and conclude that the coordinates commute as $N \to \infty$. How many "cells" of
area does the unit sphere have at fixed $N$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Dividing @eq-vcr-fuzzy by $j(j + 1)$ gives the stated commutator, whose size $1/\sqrt{j(j + 1)} \approx 2/N \to 0$. The
eigenvalues of $x_3$ are $N$ latitudes (@fig-vcr-equivariant), which divide the area $4\pi$ into $N$ bands of area
about $4\pi/N$: the fuzzy sphere is a sphere with $N$ quantum cells, as a spin-$j$ state occupies one of $2j + 1$
orientations.
:::

The vacuum $\phi_a = J_a$ breaks the gauge group, and Schur's lemma says to what. The last exercise uses it to find the
unbroken group of an irreducible fuzzy sphere.

::: {#exr-vcr-fz-schur}
#### The unbroken gauge group

In the vacuum $\phi_a = J_a$ with $J_a$ irreducible of dimension $N$, the unbroken gauge transformations $U \in U(N)$
satisfy $U\phi_aU^\dagger = \phi_a$. Use Schur's lemma to show that only the overall phases survive. What survives for
$\phi_a = J_a^{(N - n)} \oplus 0_n$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U$ commutes with an irreducible set $\{J_a\}$, so by Schur's lemma $U = e^{i\alpha}\mathbb{1}$: $SU(N)$ is broken
completely and only the decoupled $U(1)$ remains. For $J^{(N - n)} \oplus 0_n$ the commutant consists of $e^{i\alpha}
\mathbb{1}_{N - n} \oplus V$ with $V \in U(n)$, so $SU(N)$ breaks to $SU(n) \times U(1)$, the pattern of @exm-vcr-fz-vacuum.
:::
::::

### Vacua of the symmetric schemes

The equivariant potential @eq-vcr-equivariant-potential and the fuzzy-sphere potential are both squares, and their
minima can be found by completing the square. The proposition collects the results for $m = 1$, for the equal-rank
vacua of every $m$, and for the fuzzy sphere, with the mass spectra that follow.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcr-symmetric-vacua}
#### Vacua of the equivariant and fuzzy potentials

(i) For $m = 1$ with a $k_0 \times k_1$ Higgs field $\phi$, $k_0 \geq k_1$, and $c = 1/4g^2R^2$,
$$
V = \frac{g^2}2\operatorname{tr}(c - \phi\phi^\dagger)^2 + \frac{g^2}2\operatorname{tr}(\phi^\dagger\phi - c)^2 =
\frac{(k_0 - k_1)g^2c^2}{2} + g^2\operatorname{tr}(c - \phi^\dagger\phi)^2 ,
$$ {#eq-vcr-m1-potential}
minimal at $\phi^0 = \frac1{2gR}\binom{0}{\mathbb{1}_{k_1}}$ with $V = (k_0 - k_1)/(32g^2R^4)$ [@dolan2009, eqs. 4.4-4.6].
(ii) For $k_0 = k_1 = 1$ the Higgs mass is $\mu_h = 1/R$, with one Goldstone boson. (iii) For $(k_0, k_1) = (2, 1)$ the
vector mass matrix of @dolan2009 [eq. 4.17] has eigenvalues $0$, $\frac1{8R^2}$ (twice) and $\frac1{2R^2}$: $\mu_Z =
2\mu_W$, the photon is $\frac12(\sqrt3W^3 + B)$ and $\sin^2\theta_W = \tfrac34$. (iv) For equal ranks $k_i = 1$ the
vacuum $\phi_i^0 = \sqrt{i(m - i + 1)}/(2gR)$ solves $[\boldsymbol\phi, \boldsymbol\phi^\dagger] =
\boldsymbol\Sigma/4g^2R^2$ for $m = 1, \dots, 5$ [@dolan2009, eq. 3.11]. (v) The spin matrices satisfy @eq-vcr-fuzzy,
and $F_{ab}$ and the fuzzy potential vanish at $\phi_a = J_a$, for $N = 2, \dots, 6$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/vcr_equivariant.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The abelian case is the Mexican hat, and the proposition fixes its scales in terms of the radius. The first example
compares the Higgs and vector masses.

::: {#exm-vcr-sv-abelian}
#### Scales of the abelian model

For $k_0 = k_1 = 1$ the vacuum $|\phi| = 1/2gR$ gives the Higgs mass $\mu_h = 1/R$ and, from the gauge mass matrix
of @dolan2009 [eq. 4.10], a massive vector $B$ with $\mu_B^2 = 1/2R^2$: $\mu_h = \sqrt2\mu_B$, and every mass is fixed
by the radius of the sphere, with no free parameter in the potential [@dolan2009, eq. 4.21].
:::

With unequal blocks the vacuum energy is positive and the breaking is more intricate. The example spells out the
numbers for the $SU(3)$ case of @exm-vcr-eq-su3.

::: {#exm-vcr-sv-su3}
#### The $SU(3)$ case

For $(k_0, k_1) = (2, 1)$, $V_{\min} = 1/(32g^2R^4) > 0$ (@exr-vcr-eq-trace), the Higgs boson has $\mu_h = 1/R$
(@exr-vcr-sv-sage-higgs), the $W^\pm$ have $\mu_W = 1/(2\sqrt2R)$ and the $Z$ has $\mu_Z = 1/(\sqrt2R)$, so $\mu_h =
\sqrt2\mu_Z = 2\sqrt2\mu_W$ [@dolan2009, eq. 4.21]. The ratio $\mu_W/\mu_Z = \cos\theta_W = \tfrac12$ is the
$\sin^2\theta_W = \tfrac34$ of the proposition.
:::

For $m = 2$ the vacuum involves two Higgs fields that must align. The example gives it and the two Higgs masses that
@exr-vcr-sv-m2-masses computes.

::: {#exm-vcr-sv-m2}
#### $m = 2$

With $k_0 = k_1 = k_2 = 1$ the charges are $(2, 0, -2)$ and (iv) gives $\phi_1^0 = \phi_2^0 = 1/(\sqrt2gR)$, which
breaks $U(1)^2$ (after removing the overall $U(1)$) completely with $V = 0$. The two Higgs bosons have masses $\sqrt3/R$
and $1/R$ [@dolan2009, eq. 5.7], the radial modes of the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of $\phi_1$ and
$\phi_2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The identity @eq-vcr-m1-potential locates the minimum by inspection. The first exercise asks for the proof, which
uses only the cyclicity of the trace.

::: {#exr-vcr-sv-minimum}
#### Completing the square

Prove @eq-vcr-m1-potential using $\operatorname{tr}(\phi\phi^\dagger)^n = \operatorname{tr}(\phi^\dagger\phi)^n$, and
deduce that the minimum is attained when $\phi^\dagger\phi = c\,\mathbb{1}_{k_1}$, for example at $\phi^0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding, $\operatorname{tr}(c - \phi\phi^\dagger)^2 = k_0c^2 - 2c\operatorname{tr}\phi\phi^\dagger +
\operatorname{tr}(\phi\phi^\dagger)^2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\phi^\dagger\phi - c)^2 = \operatorname{tr}(\phi^\dagger
\phi)^2 - 2c\operatorname{tr}\phi^\dagger\phi + k_1c^2$. With the trace identities the sum is $(k_0 - k_1)c^2 +
2\operatorname{tr}(c - \phi^\dagger\phi)^2$, and multiplying by $g^2/2$ gives the identity. The second term is a sum of
squares of the eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix $c - \phi^\dagger\phi$, minimal (zero) when $\phi^\dagger\phi =
c\mathbb{1}$, which $\phi^0$ satisfies; then $V = (k_0 - k_1)g^2c^2/2 = (k_0 - k_1)/(32g^2R^4)$.
:::

The physical spectrum comes from expanding the potential to second order around the vacuum. The second exercise does
this in Sage for the $SU(3)$ case and counts the Goldstone bosons.

::: {#exr-vcr-sv-sage-higgs}
#### The Higgs mass for $(k_0, k_1) = (2, 1)$

With Sage, expand $V = g^2(|\phi|^2 - c)^2 + g^2c^2/2$ around $\phi^0 = (0, 1/2gR)$ in canonically normalised real
fluctuations, and find the eigenvalues of the mass-squared matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
One eigenvalue is $1/R^2$, the Higgs boson with $\mu_h = 1/R$; the other three vanish, the Goldstone bosons
(@def-goldstone-boson) eaten by $W^\pm$ and $Z$ in the Higgs mechanism, as the count $4 = 1 + 3$ requires:

{{< sage exr-vcr-sv-sage-higgs >}}
:::

For $m = 2$ the potential has a quartic cross term between the two Higgs fields. The last exercise expands
@eq-vcr-equivariant-potential, checks the potential of Dolan and Szabo, and computes the two Higgs masses.

::: {#exr-vcr-sv-m2-masses}
#### Two Higgs fields

With Sage, expand @eq-vcr-equivariant-potential for $m = 2$, $k_i = 1$, compare with $V = \frac{1}{4g^2R^4} -
\frac{|\phi_1|^2 + |\phi_2|^2}{2R^2} + g^2(|\phi_1|^4 - |\phi_1|^2|\phi_2|^2 + |\phi_2|^4)$ [@dolan2009, eq. 5.3 with
$n = 1$], and find the masses around the vacuum $\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 1/(\sqrt2gR)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The expansion agrees; for $n > 1$ the expansion of @eq-vcr-equivariant-potential gives the cross term
$-g^2\operatorname{tr}(\phi_1^\dagger\phi_1\,\phi_2\phi_2^\dagger)$, the only ordering in which the matrix sizes of
the blocks match. The radial mass matrix is $\frac1{R^2}
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ with eigenvalues $\frac3{R^2}$ and $\frac1{R^2}$, the masses $\sqrt3/R$
and $1/R$, and the two phases are Goldstone bosons:

{{< sage exr-vcr-sv-m2-masses >}}
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-consistent-reductions-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three exercises below combine the sections of the chapter. The first compares the mechanisms that make each
reduction consistent, the second confronts the Freund-Rubin vacuum with its own Kaluza-Klein tower, and the third
compares the mass scales that the different schemes produce from the size of the internal space.

::: {#exr-vcr-int-ladder}
#### Why each reduction is consistent

For each of the reductions of this chapter, the torus, the Scherk-Schwarz twist on $S^1$, the group manifold $SU(2)$,
the $S^7$ truncation of eleven-dimensional supergravity, CSDR on $S^2$ and the equivariant reduction on
$\mathbb{C}P^1$, name the group whose singlets are kept, or say that there is none, and state what guarantees the
consistency of the truncation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Torus: $U(1)^n$ translations (@def-vcr-torus-reduction). Twisted circle: translations combined with the compensating
symmetry $e^{-cM}$ (@exr-vcr-sfs-ss-as-symmetric). Group manifold: $G_L$, which commutes with the gauged $G_R$
(@exm-vcr-singlet-group). In these three @thm-vcr-singlet-consistency applies. $S^7$: no symmetry of eleven-dimensional
supergravity has the $SO(8)$ gauge fields as singlets; consistency rests on cancellations between metric and four-form
(@exm-vcr-cst-s7), made manifest only in exceptional field theory, where the truncation is a generalised Scherk-Schwarz
reduction (@prp-vcr-sphere-criterion and the paragraph before it). CSDR and the equivariant reduction: $SU(2)$ acting on
the sphere combined with gauge or bundle transformations (@def-vcr-symmetric-field-scheme), a singlet truncation of the
gauge theory on the fixed sphere; the gravitational sector is not reduced. The contrast is Pauli's sphere
(@exm-vcr-singlet-pauli), where neither a symmetry nor a cancellation exists.
:::

The Freund-Rubin vacuum is a solution, but a theory on it that keeps only the massless fields must be separated from
the massive modes to be useful. The second exercise computes the lightest scalar harmonic of $S^7$ and compares it with
the curvature of $AdS_4$.

::: {#exr-vcr-int-scales}
#### No separation of scales

With SageManifolds, show that the restriction of $x_1x_2$ to the round $S^7$ of radius $a$ is an eigenfunction of the
Laplacian with eigenvalue $-16/a^2 = -l(l + 6)/a^2$, $l = 2$. With $a = 1/m$ and $L = 1/2m$, compare the Kaluza-Klein
scale $16/a^2$ with the anti-de Sitter scale $1/L^2$, and explain why the result does not depend on the flux.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The ratio is $16m^2/4m^2 = 4$ for every $m$: both scales are set by the single parameter $m$ (@prp-vcr-freund-rubin-geometry
fixes $a = 2L$), so the massive harmonics are never much heavier than the curvature scale of spacetime.
Freund-Rubin vacua have no separation between the four-dimensional and the internal scales; the truncation to the
massless $N = 8$ multiplet is consistent, but it is not a low-energy approximation:

{{< sage exr-vcr-int-scales >}}
:::

Every scheme of this chapter ties the four-dimensional masses to the size of the internal space. The last exercise puts
the results side by side.

::: {#exr-vcr-int-masses}
#### Masses from the internal radius

Collect, in units of the internal radius $R$ (or $a$), the lightest non-zero masses of: a Scherk-Schwarz twisted scalar
on a circle of radius $R$ with the half twist; the Higgs boson of the $m = 1$, $k_0 = k_1 = 1$ equivariant reduction
over a sphere of radius $R$; and the first massive harmonic of $AdS_4 \times S^7$ with $a = R$. Which scheme can make
a mass parametrically lighter than $1/R$, and how?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Half twist: $1/2R$ (@exm-vcr-twisted-half). Equivariant: $\mu_h = 1/R$ (@prp-vcr-symmetric-vacua). Freund-Rubin: the
$l = 2$ harmonic has $16/R^2$ in the Laplacian, so a mass of order $4/R$ (@exr-vcr-int-scales). Only the Scherk-Schwarz
twist has a continuous parameter: $M_0 = |\omega|$ for $|\omega| \leq 1/2R$ can be made arbitrarily small by a small
twist (@prp-vcr-twisted-spectrum), which is how Scherk-Schwarz breaking of supersymmetry can sit below the
Kaluza-Klein scale. The geometric and equivariant masses are fixed multiples of $1/R$.
:::
::::
